outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms with wind and hail are possible this afternoon and evening, over the mid/upper Mississippi Valley region and the southern High Plains and nearby Borderlands.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: In mid/upper levels, a split-flow pattern will persist across the CONUS, characterized synoptically by: 1. A nearly zonal northern stream over the states adjoining the border with Canada, upstream from an elongated/large cyclone covering parts of Hudson Bay and QC. An embedded shortwave trough -- evident in moisture-channel imagery over the Dakotas -- contains a couple vorticity maxima, one being an MCV near DVL. This perturbation should move east-southeastward over parts of the upper Great Lakes through 12Z. 2. A broad and persistent, but not very intense, cyclone initially centered near YUM. This feature should move slowly eastward across the southern AZ region, reaching the southern part of the AZ/NM line near the end of the period. At the surface, 11Z analysis showed a wavy, quasistationary frontal zone over parts of eastern SC westward over northern portions of GA/AL. A low was analyzed near the SK/MB/ND border confluence, with cold front across northern MT. The southeastern front should move little through the period, while weakening. sections.title: Mid/upper Mississippi Valley region
sections.text: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms should develop mainly in the warm sector, within a broad area from portions of MN/WI through the lower Missouri Valley and Ozarks. Large hail and sporadic severe gusts are possible. Clustering of some of this activity should occur, especially across parts of MN. In that area, slightly stronger flow aloft, with greater low-level convergence and deep lift ahead of the low and MCV, may contribute to cold-pool development, forward-propagational maintenance and related strong-severe wind potential, for at least a few hours late this afternoon into evening. The convective/severe threat will be more patchy in nature within the outlook than can be depicted by these lines. Outside a more- confident threat for upscale aggregation over parts of MN and northern WI ahead of the MCV, uncertainty in position/strength of mesoscale foci necessitates maintaining a rather broad-brushed approach pending trends observable through the day, and after model cycles become available that incorporate 12Z RAOBs. sections.title: Southern High Plains/Borderlands/Trans Pecos
sections.text: Scattered to locally numerous thunderstorms are expected to form again today from the desert Borderlands area of southern NM and far west TX, across the higher terrain from the Big Bend to southeastern NM, and over parts of the adjoining southern Great Plains. Damaging gusts and large hail will be the main concerns. Coverage farther north into the central High Plains will be more isolated to widely scattered, but still locally clustered, with isolated severe gusts/ hail also possible. Tornado potential will be very isolated, brief, and conditional on mainly storm-scale processes and boundary interactions. Difluent, broadly cyclonic midlevel flow is expected ahead of the slowly progressive cyclone, but weaker in magnitude than preceding days. Upper-level (near anvil-level) flow will be strongest over far west TX and southeastern NM, to the lower Pecos Valley. As such, deep shear should decrease northward over the southern/central High Plains. Sufficient deep shear will remain across parts of eastern NM and west TX to support at least fleeting supercellular characteristics, especially during the first 2-3 hours of the convective cycle, before a lack of substantial MLCINH leads to ups

sections.title: Eastern GA/SC...northeastern FL
sections.text: Scattered thunderstorms should form this afternoon along and south of the front, offering marginally severe gusts and hail, along with more numerous subsevere gusts still capable of minor damage. Although low/middle-level flow will be weak, forecast soundings reasonably show backed surface flow and pronounced veering of winds with height. This will contribute to some enhancement of deep-layer shear, despite the smallness of low-level hodographs, with effective-shear magnitudes 40-45 kt possible. As such, a blend of organized multicells and transient supercells is possible across this region, especially over the coastal plain where low-level moisture will remain relatively maximized. Surface dew points should remain in the mid 60s to low 70s in the outlook area amidst strong diurnal heating, contributing to preconvective MLCAPE in the 1500-2500 J/kg range. Buoyancy will decrease westward into more deeply mixed, drier air, and northward past the front. ..Edwards/Goss.. 06/04/2019

outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms with wind and hail are possible this afternoon and evening, over the mid/upper Mississippi Valley region, the southern High Plains, and portions of Georgia/South Carolina.

sections.title: Midwest and Upper MS Valley
sections.text: Water vapor imagery suggests multiple upper systems that will affect this region. One is over the western Dakotas, and should continue to foster thunderstorm development across MN through the day. Slow moistening/destabilization will occur over central/eastern MN with convection likely intensifying to occasionally severe levels. Hail should be a primary risk with these early storms. Given the early start and relatively weak shear profiles, convection should transition to linear modes by mid-afternoon. Activity will track across much of WI this evening with bowing structures expected - capable of damaging wind gusts. It is unclear how far east this activity will maintain intensity, but have extended SLGT to include the remainder of eastern WI given trends in recent CAMs. Second shortwave trough is over KS/OK and will track into MO today. A consensus of 12z CAM solutions develop clusters of thunderstorms ahead of this system, but there is considerable spread in the details of initiation and evolution. sections.title: Southeast NM and Southwest TX
sections.text: Relatively widespread thunderstorm activity is forecast again today over parts of southeast NM into Southwest TX. Storms will form over northern Mexico and spread east-northeastward across the region late this afternoon and evening. Similar to the past several days, the strongest cells will pose a threat for damaging winds and hail.

sections.title: GA/SC
sections.text: Strong heating is occurring today over parts of southeast GA and coastal SC, where a very moist and unstable air mass has developed. Southeasterly low-level winds, beneath the southern fringe of stronger westerlies, is creating a sufficient vertical shear profile for a few severe storms this afternoon. Steep low-level lapse rates and cool temperatures aloft will promote a risk of hail and damaging winds in the strongest cells. ..Hart/Wendt.. 06/04/2019

outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms with wind and hail remain possible this afternoon and evening over the mid/upper Mississippi Valley region, the southern High Plains, and portions of Georgia/South Carolina.

sections.title: 20Z Update
sections.text: The Enhanced risk for strong/damaging winds has been expanded across parts of southern MN based on recent radar trends. A MCS developing across central MN this afternoon should continue generally southeastward into southern MN by this evening. Low-level lapse rates have steepened ahead of this convection, which should encourage efficient mixing of convective downdrafts to the surface. For more information on the short-term severe threat across this region, see Mesoscale Discussion 976. The Marginal risk area has been expanded slightly westward across the Dakotas to account for recent thunderstorm development along and just ahead of a weak cold front. Convection should continue to increase in coverage through the rest of the afternoon, with an isolated hail/wind threat with the strongest updrafts. Modest shear will probably tend to limit a greater severe weather threat. Otherwise, only minor changes have been made to severe probabilities across parts of western MO behind an eastward-moving MCV. ..Gleason.. 06/04/2019 .PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1113 AM CDT Tue Jun 04 2019/

sections.title: Southeast NM and Southwest TX
sections.text: Relatively widespread thunderstorm activity is forecast again today over parts of southeast NM into Southwest TX. Storms will form over northern Mexico and spread east-northeastward across the region late this afternoon and evening. Similar to the past several days, the strongest cells will pose a threat for damaging winds and hail.

sections.title: GA/SC
sections.text: Strong heating is occurring today over parts of southeast GA and coastal SC, where a very moist and unstable air mass has developed. Southeasterly low-level winds, beneath the southern fringe of stronger westerlies, is creating a sufficient vertical shear profile for a few severe storms this afternoon. Steep low-level lapse rates and cool temperatures aloft will promote a risk of hail and damaging winds in the strongest cells.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Scattered thunderstorms are expected to develop from southeast Georgia through southern South Carolina by 18Z. Downburst winds will be the main threat, but some hail is also possible through much of the afternoon. Trends are being monitored for a possible WW.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Early this afternoon, strong destabilization of the surface layer is occurring from southeast GA to southern SC where temperatures range from mid 80s to near 90F. Despite weak mid-level lapse rates around 5.5-6 C/km, rich low-level moisture and strong diabatic warming are promoting 1500-2000 J/kg MLCAPE in vicinity of a stalled boundary. A few showers have already developed near the SC coast, and convergence along the stalled front as well as the seabreeze should support thunderstorm initiation within the next hour. Moreover, RAP analysis and WV imagery indicate a shortwave trough over the southern Appalachians moving southeast toward this region. Easterly low-level winds associated with circulation around an area of high pressure off the Atlantic seaboard beneath modest westerly flow aloft has resulted in 30-35 kt surface-6 km shear, suggesting predominantly multicell storm modes, but some weak mid-level updraft rotation may also occur within the stronger cells.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A cluster of initially elevated thunderstorms will be capable of a few larger hail stones given steep mid-level lapse rates. A greater threat for severe, particularly damaging wind gusts, will exist as the upstream airmass destabilizes by early/mid afternoon. A WW is likely going to be needed by early afternoon. With some remaining uncertainty regarding when storm intensity will increase, trends will continue to be monitored.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A small cluster of thunderstorms in west-central Minnesota has developed in association with a remnant MCV in eastern North Dakota. These storms appear to be somewhat elevated given the MLCIN still present. However, 12Z ABR sounding showed near 8 C/km lapse rates which would support a threat for a few larger hail stones. A few stronger/deeper convective cores have shown 1-1.5 inch MRMS values in the last half hour. While this activity will likely remain marginal severe in the near term, heating/moistening of the boundary layer ahead of this cluster will eventually lead to these storms becoming surface based and more intense. Dewpoints in east-central Minnesota have risen the the low 60s F in the last few hours and with upper 60s F in southern Minnesota will likely increase further by mid-afternoon. Storm organization will be limited with only 25-30 kts of effective deep-layer shear, but moderate MLCAPE of 2000-2500 J/kg by afternoon will still allow severe storms capable of large hail and, primarily, damaging wind gusts. A WW will likely be needed by early afternoon, but some uncertainty exists with when these storms will become surface based. Trends will continue to be monitored for an increase in storm intensity/coverage.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Visible satellite imagery depicts increasing cumulus activity in far western Missouri. The boundary layer is becoming increasing destabilized in central/eastern Missouri. Though timing of storm initiation is still uncertain, moderate buoyancy will support a damaging wind gust threat as well as marginally severe hail with any storms this afternoon. A WW is possible as timing becomes more clear.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: As a weak MCV/upstream shortwave trough approaches from the southwest, elevated cumulus have developed in far east-central Kansas/far western Missouri. Ahead of the MCV, dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s F have moved into much of central and eastern Missouri supporting a modestly buoyant airmass with 1000 to near 1500 J/kg MLCAPE. With continued heating/moistening, MLCAPE is forecast to rise to around 2000 J/kg by late afternoon. HREF guidance is insistent that a cluster of storms will develop in the central Missouri vicinity by 3-4 PM CDT. Observational trends would certainly support the agitated cumulus moving into central Missouri, deepening, and becoming more intense. The main uncertainty is the exact timing of when this development will occur, though recent objective mesoanalysis suggests MLCIN is near or very near being removed. Weak deep-layer shear will keep storms relatively disorganized, but moderate buoyancy will support a threat for damaging wind gusts and marginally severe hail. Watch issuance is possible in the next few hours once observational trends on storm initiation become more clear.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms may produce isolated downburst winds and marginally severe hail as they spread east off the higher terrain this afternoon into the early evening. At this time, coverage of severe events is not expected to be sufficient to warrant a WW, but trends will continue to be monitored.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: This afternoon strong diabatic heating over the mountains has resulted in thunderstorm development from northern NM, central CO, and southeast WY. Other storms are developing farther northeast into southwest SD along southwestern extension of a cold front and in association with an MCV. Downstream across the High Plains, low-level dewpoints have mixed down into the 40s to low 50s F within a steep lapse rate environment, promoting modest instability with 500-1000 J/kg MLCAPE. Surface winds have shifted to northwesterly behind a lee trough situated over the Plains, and flow aloft will remain modest resulting in 20-30 kt effective shear supportive of multicell storms. Activity will continue spreading east into the high plains with a mix of discrete storms and clusters. The steep lapse rates with inverted-V boundary layers will promote a risk for isolated downburst winds with this activity through early evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms coverage is expected to gradually increase across southeast NM through southwest Texas this afternoon into early evening with downburst winds and large hail possible. Trends in storm coverage and intensity will be monitored for a possible WW by 21 or 22Z.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Southeasterly low-level winds have maintained a fetch of richer low-level moisture across southwest TX and southeast NM with mid 50s to around 60 F dewpoints. The boundary layer continues to destabilize with strong diabatic heating and steep (8 C/km 700-500 mb) lapse rates resulting in 1500 J/kg MLCAPE. Numerous storms are initiating over the mountains of northern Mexico with more isolated development over southeast NM. Additional storms should form over the mountains of southwest TX. Despite veering low-level winds, flow through the lowest few kilometers is weak at generally 5-10 kt, but increasing to 30-40 kt around 400 mb. Some increase in mid-level winds may occur as the upper trough over the southwest U.S. moves slowly east, but overall multicell storms are expected with some marginal supercell structures also possible. Storm modes will be initially discrete, but some of this activity may consolidate into lines or clusters and subsequently propagate eastward this evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Two thunderstorm complexes are ongoing in WW 325. Much of the WW area has suffered from remaining MLCIN with the exception of a few areas where greater heating has occurred. Lack of low-level momentum/shear will likely mean outflow moves ahead of the convection in many areas. A threat for damaging wind gusts and marginally severe hail will continue where moderate buoyancy exists.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Two thunderstorm complexes are ongoing in WW 325. A well-developed bowing segment in central Minnesota is moving southeast and is expected to impact the Twin Cities metro between 3-4 PM CDT. The 18Z MPX sounding showed significant MLCIN of around 200 J/kg and a general lack of low-level momentum. Recent KMPX radar imagery has also shown outflow beginning to race ahead of the bowing segment. These observational trends would suggest that the potential for damaging wind gusts have decreased to a degree in east-central Minnesota. Temperatures in south-central Minnesota have warmed to near 90 F with upper 60s dewpoints. A relatively higher threat for damaging wind gusts will exist ahead of this activity given the steep low-level lapse rates. Farther north in the Minnesota Arrowhead, another complex of thunderstorms is beginning to push south-southeastward along the buoyancy gradient. While the 18Z INL sounding showed less capping relative to farther south, the same lack of low-level shear exists. The overall evolution of these complexes is unclear given the so-far limited buoyancy downstream in Wisconsin and the stabilization that will occur behind the complex in central Minnesota. Pockets of heating, particularly in southern Minnesota, will still support 1500-2000 J/kg MLCAPE with an attendant threat for damaging wind gusts and marginally severe hail. ..Wendt.. 06/04/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Threat for mainly isolated downburst winds will continue through early evening across southeast Georgia through southern South Carolina.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Numerous storms have developed across southeast GA through southern SC along a stalled front and sea breeze boundaries where the atmosphere has become moderately unstable with 2000 J/kg MLCAPE. VWP data from Charleston show veering low-level wind profiles with 40 kt surface-6km shear, and some supercell structures continue to be observed with the stronger and more discrete updrafts. Locally strong to damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat, but some hail is also possible, especially with storms exhibiting mid-level updraft rotation. Primary severe threat should persist next 2-3 hours before diminishing during the early evening. ..Dial.. 06/04/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A few isolated to scattered storms are possible this afternoon as a weak cold front moves southeastward. A few instances of large hail and damaging wind gusts may occur. Given weak deep-layer shear, storms will struggle to organize. Some upscale growth may occur later this afternoon which would increase the threat for damaging wind gusts. Trends will need to be monitored for a more organized severe threat. At this time, a WW is not expected.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: With weak mid-level ascent approaching, strong heating ahead of a cold front coincident with mid to upper 60s dewpoints has helped initiate isolated thunderstorms west of Aberdeen, SD. MLCAPE of 2500-3000 J/kg and steep mid-level lapse rates will support a threat for large hail and perhaps a few damaging wind gusts. Very weak deep-layer shear will limit overall storm organization. Storms will likely struggle to maintain their intensity for longer durations. Should this activity congeal, a more organized damaging wind gust threat will develop. It is unclear how long any MCS that may develop would be able to maintain itself given how weak low-level shear is. Trends will continue to be monitored for any increase MCS organization. At this time, a WW is not expected.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms over Minnesota are expected to persist through evening as they travel southeastward into Iowa and far western Wisconsin. Damaging winds will be the primary concern.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Storms associated with a weak shortwave trough are currently producing strong to severe wind gusts over south-central MN where strong instability developed during the day. One cluster near the Twin Cities contains a threat of damaging winds, and should continue to the southeast along a diffuse warm front. Meanwhile, other storms were regenerating near the surface low over southwest MN. These cells may contain marginally severe hail as well as a developing wind threat as they propagate southeast into a warm air mass. As for area near and east of the warm front, southwesterly 850 mb winds of around 20 kt will maintain some degree of warm advection into the region, but little eastward progress is expected overall in the position of the instability gradient. As such, storms will likely favor south and southwestern movement toward the warmer surface air mass into IA.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The severe weather threat continues in severe thunderstorm watch 326. The primary threat will be damaging wind and isolated large hail.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Several storm clusters have developed in western portions of watch 326. These storms have been mostly unorganized with some multicellular modes. However, given the very unstable airmass (2000 to 2500 J/kg MLCAPE per RAP mesoanalysis) these storms have produced occasional severe wind and hail despite the relative lack of organization. The airmass downstream of these storms has continued to destabilize with temperatures in the mid 80s and dewpoints in the low 70s and an expanding agitated cumulus field based on visible satellite. Therefore, expect the severe weather threat to continue into the evening as these storms move east and new storms develop. Given the weak shear (less than 25 knots per RAP soundings) and lack of storm organization, in addition to the modest mid-level lapse rates (~6 C/km), expect large hail to be the secondary threat, with damaging winds as the primary threat as stronger thunderstorms collapse. ..Bentley.. 06/04/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Occasional strong to severe storms continue through the evening.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Storms in the southern High Plains have had transient stronger cores with several reports of severe hail. Expect this threat to continue given the unstable environment and mid-level lapse rates around 7.5 to 8 C/km per 00Z EPZ and MAF RAOB. The best sustained storm has been in the Davis Mountains where MESH has indicated hail in excess of 1.5 inches for over an hour. The EPZ RAOB shows 40 to 50 knots of mid-level flow which is stronger than most forecast guidance suggested. This shear profile would support greater storm organization if this mid-level flow were able to overspread the unstable warm sector in eastern New Mexico and West Texas. However, the slow progression and orientation of the upper trough will likely not allow this stronger mid-level flow to spread much farther east. The 00Z MAF sounding showed very weak mid-level flow (10 to 20 knots) which would explain why storm organization has struggled. A southeasterly low-level jet is expected to strengthen to 30 to 35 knots later this evening which may help to organize these storms into an eastward propagating MCS. However, the aforementioned lack of shear will likely limit the overall threat and preclude the need for an additional watch east of watch 327.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Areas of damaging winds remain possible within WW 328 as a line of storms moves rapidly southeast toward southwest Wisconsin and northeast Iowa. However, a new watch may not be needed if latest trends persist.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: An MCS with a history of damaging winds is currently over extreme southeast MN and is now entering southwest WI. This leading portion of the line likely contains the strongest wind gusts with fastest forward motion. Western portions of the line extend across northern IA and back into southwest MN, parallel to the flow aloft. The environment ahead of the WI portion of the bow is sufficiently unstable, with MLCAPE likely in the 1000-1500 J/kg range judging from the 00Z DVN sounding. The fast forward motion and organized cold pool may allow for a few strong to severe wind gusts near the eastern bounds of WW 328, or a bit farther eastward into southern WI. However, overall storm trends suggest decreasingly storm strength with time. Western areas will remain in close proximity to a warm, unstable air mass, with sporadic strong to severe storms moving slowly along the northwest-southeast oriented outflow boundary. ..Jewell.. 06/05/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...
